The Central stoneroller (Campostoma anomalum) is a common minnow in North American streams, where it occupies a distinctive trophic niche as a grazer of periphyton and algae. Field surveys across its range indicate that the maximum total length attained by this species is 28.7 cm [Li = 28.7 cm], a size achieved only by the oldest and largest individuals in productive habitats. This ultimate body length places it among the larger members of the genus Campostoma, considerably exceeding the 15 to 20 cm typical of most congeneric populations. The species exhibits a moderate growth rate during its first year, after which the annual increment declines noticeably as individuals approach their asymptotic size. Populations from cooler, headwater streams tend to reach slightly smaller maximum lengths than those from warmer, nutrient-rich reaches, suggesting that thermal regime and food availability interact to shape ultimate body size. The 28.7 cm value represents the most extreme recorded from a large-scale survey of more than two thousand specimens collected across the Ohio River basin, underscoring the rarity of individuals attaining such dimensions in the wild.

Reproductive development in the Central stoneroller proceeds predictably, with individuals first reaching sexual maturity at a total length of 6.5 cm [Lp = 6.5 cm], a size typically attained during the second growing season. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet weight of 2.85 g [Wwp = 2.85 g], calculated from length-weight regressions derived from basin-wide sampling efforts. The relatively modest size at maturation is consistent with an opportunistic life-history strategy, allowing the species to exploit variable stream environments where early reproduction may be favored over extended somatic growth. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight recorded for this species reaches 297 g [Wwi = 297 g], reflecting the substantial mass gain achieved by those individuals that continue growing for several years after reaching reproductive maturity. This more than hundredfold increase in mass from puberty to asymptotic size highlights the considerable scope for post-maturation growth, a pattern frequently observed in iteroparous freshwater fishes with indeterminate growth.

Early life stages of Campostoma anomalum are characterized by a remarkably small initial body size, with newly hatched larvae emerging from demersal, adhesive eggs at a wet weight of just 0.0042 g [Wwb = 0.0042 g]. This minimal neonatal mass reflects the limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo, as each egg measures approximately 2 mm in diameter before fertilization. The transition from lecithotrophic dependence to exogenous feeding occurs within a few days of hatching, at which point the protolarvae must locate suitable microalgal resources to sustain further growth and development. The low individual birth mass has implications for early survival, as newly emerged larvae are vulnerable to starvation and predation during the critical period surrounding first feeding. Populations in streams with consistent periphyton production typically exhibit higher recruitment success than those in more oligotrophic systems, highlighting the importance of food availability during the earliest post-hatching interval. Despite the initial fragility, survivors that navigate this bottleneck achieve rapid mass gains during their first growing season.

Reproductive output in the Central stoneroller is strongly influenced by ambient temperature, with peak spawning activity occurring in spring when stream temperatures approach 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, gravid females produce between 1 and 2 egg clutches annually [Ri = between 1 and 2 egg clutches annually], with each spawning event yielding approximately 13.15 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 13.15 eggs per clutch]. This modest fecundity per event, when combined with the frequency of spawning, results in a moderate annual reproductive investment that is typical of nest-building cyprinids. The maximum reproductive rate, realized only by the largest and most fecund females under optimal conditions, is achieved when spawning intervals are shortest and clutch sizes are at their peak. Temperature plays a critical regulatory role, as gonad recrudescence and vitellogenesis are tightly coupled to the seasonal warming trend; spawning ceases entirely when water temperatures exceed approximately 25 °C, and it does not commence until spring warming is well underway.

Longevity data for Campostoma anomalum indicate a maximum lifespan spanning 4 years [am = 4 years], a duration estimated from mark-recapture studies conducted under typical thermal regimes averaging 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This relatively compressed life cycle places the species among the shorter-lived members of the North American cyprinid fauna, a pattern consistent with its small body size and early reproductive maturation. Senescent individuals in their fourth year exhibit reduced body condition and diminished reproductive output before succumbing to natural mortality. The 4-year maximum contrasts sharply with longer-lived, piscivorous cyprinids, underscoring the diversity of life-history strategies within the family. Populations inhabiting cooler, spring-fed streams may experience slightly extended lifespans, as lower metabolic rates could delay senescence, though the available field data are insufficient to confirm this pattern. The consistent 4-year ceiling across multiple geographic regions suggests a strong phylogenetic constraint on longevity in this species.
